title: Electrical cable
description: Assembly of one or more wires running side by side or bundled
wiki_lead:
An electrical cable is an assembly of one or more wires running side by side or bundled, which is used as an electrical conductor to carry electric current. 
Electrical cables are used to connect two or more devices, enabling the transfer of electrical signals, power, or both from one device to the other. Physically, an electrical cable is an assembly consisting of one or more conductors with their own insulations and optional screens, individual coverings, assembly protection and protective covering.
One or more electrical cables and their corresponding connectors may be formed into a cable assembly, which is not necessarily suitable for connecting two devices but can be a partial product (e.g. to be soldered onto a printed circuit board with a connector mounted to the housing). Cable assemblies can also take the form of a cable tree or cable harness, used to connect many terminals together.

An electrical cable is an assembly of one or more wires running side by side or bundled, which is used as an electrical conductor to carry electric current. 
Electrical cables are used to connect two or more devices, enabling the transfer of electrical signals, power, or both from one device to the other. Physically, an electrical cable is an assembly consisting of one or more conductors with their own insulations and optional screens, individual coverings, assembly protection and protective covering.
One or more electrical cables and their corresponding connectors may be formed into a cable assembly, which is not necessarily suitable for connecting two devices but can be a partial product (e.g. to be soldered onto a printed circuit board with a connector mounted to the housing). Cable assemblies can also take the form of a cable tree or cable harness, used to connect many terminals together.


Uses

Electrical cables are used to connect two or more devices, enabling the transfer of electrical signals or power from one device to the other. Long-distance communication takes place over undersea communication cables. Power cables are used for bulk transmission of alternating and direct current power, especially using high-voltage cable. Electrical cables are extensively used in building wiring for lighting, power and control circuits permanently installed in buildings. Since all the circuit conductors required can be installed in a cable at one time, installation labor is saved compared to certain other wiring methods.
Physically, an electrical cable is an assembly consisting of one or more conductors with their own insulations and optional screens, individual coverings, assembly protection and protective coverings. Electrical cables may be made more flexible by stranding the wires. In this process, smaller individual wires are twisted or braided together to produce larger wires that are more flexible than solid wires of similar size. Bunching small wires before concentric stranding adds the most flexibility. Copper wires in a cable may be bare, or they may be plated with a thin layer of another metal, most often tin, but sometimes gold, silver or another material. Tin, gold, and silver are much less prone to oxidation than copper, which may lengthen wire life, and makes soldering easier. Tinning is also used to provide lubrication between strands. Tinning was used to help removal of rubber insulation. Tight lays during stranding make the cable extensible (CBA – as in telephone handset cords).
In the 19th century and early 20th century, electrical cable was often insulated using cloth, rubber or paper. Plastic materials are generally used today, except for high-reliability power cables. The first thermoplastic used was gutta-percha (a natural latex) which was found useful for underwater cables in the 19th century. The first, and still very common, man-made plastic used for cable insulation was polyethylene. This was invented in 1930, but not available outside military use until after World War 2 during which a telegraph cable using it was laid across the English Channel to support troops following D-Day. 
Cables can be securely fastened and organized, such as by using trunking, cable trays, cable ties or cable lacing. Continuous-flex or flexible cables used in moving applications within cable carriers can be secured using strain relief devices or cable ties.


Characteristics

Any current-carrying conductor, including a cable, radiates an electromagnetic field. Likewise, any conductor or cable will pick up energy from any existing electromagnetic field around it. These effects are often undesirable, in the first case amounting to unwanted transmission of energy which may adversely affect nearby equipment or other parts of the same piece of equipment; and in the second case, unwanted pickup of noise which may mask the desired signal being carried by the cable, or, if the cable is carrying power supply or control voltages, pollute
grok_lead: An electrical cable is an assembly of one or more insulated electrical conductors under a common or integral jacket, designed to safely transmit electrical power or signals between points in various systems. These cables are essential components in modern electrical infrastructure, enabling the distribution of electricity in buildings, industrial facilities, power grids, and transportation networks. Electrical cables are constructed with conductors typically made of stranded copper or aluminum for efficient current carrying, surrounded by insulation materials such as thermoplastic (e.g., PVC or XLPE) or elastomeric compounds to prevent electrical leakage and protect against environmental hazards. The outer jacket, often moisture-resistant and made from similar polymers, provides mechanical protection, while additional features like armor or shielding may be included for specific applications requiring durability or electromagnetic interference resistance. In North America, conductor sizes are standardized using the American Wire Gauge (AWG) system, where smaller numbers indicate larger diameters capable of handling higher currents, such as AWG 6 for heavy appliances or AWG 18 for lighter loads; internationally, sizes are specified by cross-sectional area in square millimeters per IEC 60228. Common types of electrical cables include non-metallic sheathed cable (NM, common in the US for residential wiring), armored cable (such as BX or AC in North America, or steel wire armored (SWA) in the UK for mechanical protection in exposed installations), and underground feeder (UF) cable for direct burial applications. Power cables operate at various voltages, from low-voltage building wiring up to 1 kV (per IEC standards) or under 600 V (per US NEC) to high-voltage transmission lines exceeding 25 kV, often using tree-retardant cross-linked polyethylene (TR-XLPE) insulation for reliability. Specialized variants, such as control cables with multiple small conductors or coaxial cables for signal transmission, support diverse uses in automation, telecommunications, and audio systems. The design, installation, and maintenance of electrical cables are governed by rigorous standards to ensure safety and performance, including the National Electrical Code (NEC) and IEEE guidelines in the US, as well as international standards from the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), such as IEC 60364 for wiring and IEC 60502 for power cables. Key considerations include fire resistance, as cable construction influences flame propagation and smoke emission in emergencies, and environmental factors like moisture or mechanical stress that can degrade insulation over time. Proper adherence to these standards minimizes risks such as electrical faults, overheating, or fire hazards, underscoring the critical role of electrical cables in reliable and safe power delivery.
